The Notchedfin threadfin bream Nemipterus peronii attains a maximum recorded standard length of approximately 29 centimeters [Li = approximately 29 centimeters], a size typically reached only by older individuals in populations subject to low fishing pressure. This ultimate length reflects the species’ position as a medium-sized member of the Nemipteridae, a family of demersal carnivores common across the continental shelves of the Indo-West Pacific. Field surveys conducted in the South China Sea indicate that the onset of gonadal development occurs when individuals reach a standard length of roughly 10 centimeters [Lp = roughly 10 centimeters], marking the transition from the juvenile to the adult phase. This size at puberty is consistent with the reproductive strategy of many iteroparous tropical fishes, which channel energy toward early maturity as a hedge against high natural mortality. Juveniles recruit to the benthic habitat after a pelagic larval phase of several weeks, during which they are vulnerable to predation and advection away from suitable nursery grounds. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that variation in the length at maturity is linked to local thermal regimes and food availability, with faster-growing cohorts in warmer, productive waters reaching puberty at a slightly smaller size than their slower-growing counterparts.

The eggs of Nemipterus peronii are small and pelagic, a common trait among nemipterids that broadcast spawn in tropical shelf waters. At the moment of fertilization, the ovum contains a minimal endowment of yolk, resulting in a hatchling wet weight at birth of only 0.000066 grams [Wwb = 0.000066 grams], which is derived from an egg diameter of approximately half a millimeter. This extremely small initial mass places the newly emerged yolk-sac larva firmly in the lecithotrophic phase, during which it relies entirely on endogenous reserves before the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding commences. The tiny size at birth imposes a narrow window for successful first prey capture; delayed onset of feeding beyond the point of no return leads to irreversible starvation and mortality within just a few days. The energetic economy of these early stages exerts a strong selective pressure on spawning timing, as larvae must encounter adequate densities of suitable microplanktonic prey immediately upon yolk absorption. Consequently, the reproductive schedule of adults is closely tied to seasonal plankton blooms and local oceanographic conditions.

Spawning activity in Nemipterus peronii is protracted across the warmer months, and the species exhibits a high daily reproductive output when measured under the typical thermal regime of its tropical habitat. At a water temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], gravid females sampled from the Gulf of Thailand at a fork length of 23.75 centimeters were found to produce roughly 527 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 527 eggs per day], a rate that reflects the continuous batch-spawning strategy common to many small-to-medium-sized lutjanoid fishes. This daily fecundity is sustained over a breeding season that spans several months, allowing a single female to release tens of thousands of eggs annually. The high reproductive rate is offset by negligible parental investment and extremely high egg and larval mortality, typical of an r-selected life-history strategy. Comparisons with other nemipterid species from cooler waters suggest that the daily egg production of Nemipterus peronii near its thermal optimum may be elevated relative to that of temperate relatives, which display slower oocyte development and lower batch frequencies. The energetic cost of such sustained gamete production is substantial and appears to constrain the ultimate size that individuals can attain.

The ultimate wet weight of Nemipterus peronii has been estimated from length-weight relationships derived from commercial catch data across its range. The largest individuals recorded in scientific surveys reach an asymptotic body mass approaching 400 grams [Wwi = 400 grams], a figure that corresponds well with the predicted weight from the species’ maximum standard length of 29 centimeters. This ultimate wet weight places the species among the smaller-bodied members of the genus, with congeneric species such as Nemipterus japonicus attaining considerably larger masses. The relationship between length and weight in this species follows an allometric exponent near three, indicating approximately isometric growth, though slight seasonal variation in condition factor has been reported in association with the reproductive cycle. Females in spawning condition often exhibit reduced condition factors due to the depletion of somatic reserves that are instead directed toward vitellogenesis and egg production. After the spawning season concludes, individuals gradually rebuild body mass through intensive feeding on benthic crustaceans and small cephalopods, restoring the energy stores needed to survive the cooler months and prepare for the next reproductive period.

The maximum lifespan of Nemipterus peronii, as inferred from otolith-based age validation studies conducted at a water temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years], a relatively short duration for a demersal teleost of its size. This longevity is consistent with the rapid life-history pace of tropical fishes, which typically exhibit higher metabolic rates, earlier maturity, and shorter lifespans than temperate or cold-water species. The oldest individuals in the studied populations rarely exceed this 6-year threshold, suggesting that senescence and natural mortality impose a firm upper bound on survival even in the absence of fishing. Growth curves fitted to mark-recapture data indicate that most asymptotic size is achieved within the first three to four years, after which somatic growth slows considerably and energy is redirected toward reproduction. The short lifespan, combined with early maturity and high fecundity, classifies this species as an opportunistic strategist well adapted to the variable and predation-rich environment of tropical shelf ecosystems. Fishing pressure, which selectively removes larger, older individuals, likely truncates the age structure further, reducing the average lifespan well below the physiological maximum.
